stemMd:
Two years ago a logistics firm introduced a four-day working week. Since then, annual staff turnover at the firm has fallen from 14 percent to 6 percent. The firm's human-resources director concludes that the four-day week has made employees more loyal to the firm.

Which of the following, if true, most weakens the director's conclusion?

options.label: A
options.textMd: The firm's salaries are similar to those paid by its main competitors.

options.label: B
options.textMd: Employees say they are more satisfied with their working hours than they were before the change.

options.label: C
options.textMd: Over the same two years, the number of vacancies advertised in the firm's sector fell by more than half.

options.label: D
options.textMd: The firm hired temporary staff to cover the work that used to be done on the fifth day.

options.label: E
options.textMd: During the ten years before the change, the firm's turnover stayed close to 14 percent every year.

explanationMd:
The director sees two things happen together, a shorter week and lower turnover, and concludes that the first caused the second by making employees loyal. To weaken a causal claim, offer another cause for the same effect, or break the link.

When there are far fewer job vacancies in the sector, staff have fewer places to go, so turnover falls whether or not they feel loyal. The fall from 14 to 6 percent could then have happened even without the four-day week, and without any change in loyalty. That is the alternative explanation, and it is supplied by the choice about vacancies falling by more than half.

Check the other four: satisfaction with hours and a steady earlier turnover both **support** the director; similar salaries and temporary cover for the fifth day are irrelevant to why staff stay.

distractorRationale.b: It sounds like a comment on the change, so it can be mistaken for a challenge to it, but it strengthens the conclusion by giving a reason why employees might now prefer to stay.
distractorRationale.a: It looks like a rival explanation based on pay, but pay that matches the competitors' did not change and does not explain why turnover fell. It neither explains the fall nor undermines the director's account of it.
distractorRationale.e: Historical data can look like a challenge, but this strengthens the conclusion. A steady earlier rate makes it harder to say that the drop is just random variation or a long-running trend, and points to the change as the cause.
distractorRationale.d: It may look like a hidden cost or side effect of the change, but a drawback of the policy is not evidence against its effect on loyalty. This concerns how the work gets done, not why permanent employees leave or stay, so it does not touch the link between the shorter week and turnover.

accessibilityText: An argument question about weakening a conclusion. A logistics firm introduced a four-day week two years ago. Annual staff turnover fell from 14 percent to 6 percent. The human-resources director concludes that the four-day week made employees more loyal. The question asks which statement most weakens this conclusion. The choices: employees are more satisfied with their hours; salaries are similar to competitors'; sector vacancies fell by more than half over the same two years; turnover had stayed close to 14 percent for the ten years before the change; temporary staff cover the fifth-day work.

provenance.notes: Original item written for this bank. Scenario, names and figures are invented; no published TOLC or other test item was used or adapted.

review.author: tolc-e-wave6-author

independentSolve.workingNotes: C offers an alternative cause: sector vacancies fell by more than half, so staff had fewer chances to leave, which explains lower turnover without greater loyalty. E rules out a prior trend and so strengthens the conclusion. B also strengthens it. A and D do not bear on why people stay. [A second, separate blind solve (blind-reviewer-wave6-tolce-logic-run5) reached the same answer: C gives another explanation: fewer outside vacancies means fewer chances to leave, so turnover would fall even without extra loyalty. E strengthens by ruling out a pre-existing trend. B mildly supports. A and D do not bear on why turnover fell.]

review.notes: Uniqueness check: only the fall in sector vacancies offers a rival cause for lower turnover. Two choices strengthen the claim and two are irrelevant to it. Options were reordered after review to remove answer-position bias; ids and labels were remapped with the key.
